result.summary: Juno, angry at Ino's good fortune, descends to the underworld and sends the Fury Tisiphone to drive Athamas and Ino mad. Athamas kills his son Learchus and Ino leaps into the sea with Melicerta, and Neptune makes them sea gods at Venus's request. Ino's attendants are turned to stone or birds.

scenes.title: Juno resents Ino's happiness
scenes.summary: Summary lines announce the tale, then Juno sees Ino prospering and resolves to use madness against her, as Bacchus did with Pentheus.
scenes.stakes: Juno's pride: she fears being powerless to avenge herself on those who despise her.

scenes.title: Juno descends to the underworld
scenes.summary: Juno goes down past Cerberus, sees the damned, and commands the Furies to destroy Athamas. Tisiphone agrees and Juno returns, purified by Iris.
scenes.stakes: Athamas and his house are marked for destruction by Juno's hatred.

scenes.title: Tisiphone maddens Athamas and Ino
scenes.summary: Tisiphone arrives at the palace and casts snakes and poison into the couple. Athamas, believing he hunts lions, dashes Learchus against stones, and Ino flees with Melicerta.
scenes.stakes: Ino and Athamas lose their reason; their children face death.

scenes.title: Ino leaps; Neptune makes them gods
scenes.summary: Ino throws herself and Melicerta from a sea cliff. Venus pleads with Neptune, who makes them the sea deities Leucothoë and Palæmon.

scenes.title: Ino's attendants transformed
scenes.summary: The Theban women lament and blame Juno, who turns them into stone or birds.
scenes.stakes: The attendants suffer Juno's punishment for reproaching her.

Melicerta's new divine name after becoming a sea god.
Ino's name as a sea goddess.

notable_quotes.reason: Juno admits it is right to learn even from an enemy.
Vivid statement that the Fury's wounds strike the mind, not the body.

analysis.text: Divine jealousy and vengeance destroy the house of Cadmus; madness is a weapon of the gods and Bacchus's example inspires Juno.
Metamorphosis follows suffering, turning victims into gods, rocks or birds.

legacy.text: Ino as the sea goddess Leucothea appears in Homer's Odyssey, helping Ulysses, and Dante's Inferno draws on the Athamas madness episode.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's underworld here is a vivid description borrowed and adapted from Virgil's Aeneid and Greek tradition.

language_notes.text: His aunt is Ino, sister of Semele, Bacchus's mother. The 'sisters' are Semele, Agave and Autonoe, whose sorrows came from Semele's death and Pentheus's destruction.
Ino nursed the infant Bacchus after Semele's death, so he is Juno's hated 'foster-child' of Ino; Athamas is Ino's husband, king in Thebes' region.
Child of a concubine: Bacchus, son of Jupiter and the mortal Semele. 'Mæonian sailors' are the Tyrrhenian pirates turned into dolphins by Bacchus.
The mother tearing her son is Agave killing Pentheus; the daughters of Minyas, who spurned Bacchus's rites, were changed into bats (the 'wings').
Pentheus, king of Thebes, resisted Bacchus and was torn apart by his own mother and aunts in a frenzy sent by the god.
Styx is the main river of the underworld; "languid" describes its sluggish, stagnant flow. "New-made ghosts" are the recently dead.
Adamant is a legendary unbreakable metal, here used for the prison's doors.
Tityus was a giant punished for assaulting Latona; vultures eternally tear at his liver, which regrows. His body covers nine acres.
Tantalus is punished by thirst and hunger: water and fruit recede whenever he reaches for them.
Ixion, who tried to seduce Juno, is bound to a revolving wheel; he "flies from himself" as the wheel carries him round.
The Belides, the Danaids, killed their cousins on their wedding night and must forever fill leaking vessels.
Purification by sprinkled water cleanses Juno of the pollution of contact with the dead.
Tisiphone is one of the Furies, avenging goddesses of the underworld; 'persecuting' reflects her role as punisher.
'Æolian' means belonging to Æolus, Athamas's ancestor; the house is of Æolus's line.
Erinnys is the Greek name for a Fury; here it is another name for Tisiphone.
Cerberus is the three-headed dog guarding the underworld; Echidna is a serpent-bodied monster, mother of many monsters. Their venom makes the potion infernal.
Pluto is the ruler of the underworld; 'empty realms' means the realm of the dead.
'Evoë, Bacche' is the ritual cry of Bacchus's frenzied worshippers; Ino, mad, mistakes herself for a Bacchante.
Juno mocks Ino, who had nursed the infant Bacchus (Semele's son, whom Juno hated); 'foster-child' is Bacchus.
Venus calls Ino her granddaughter because Ino's mother Harmonia was Venus's daughter by Mars. Neptune is her uncle in the translator's loose family reckoning, as a sea god related to her birth.
Venus was said to be born from the sea foam; her Greek name Aphrodite is linked to the Greek word aphros, 'foam'.
Leucothoë and Palæmon are the sea deities Ino and Melicerta become; the Greeks knew them as Leucothea and Palaemon, helpers of sailors.
The 'concubine' is Semele, Cadmus's daughter and mother of Bacchus, whom Juno hated. Ino's family suffers from Juno's anger at Semele's line.
Sidonian means from Sidon in Phoenicia, the homeland of Cadmus, who came from there to found Thebes.
Ismenus is the river at Thebes, so these birds are the Theban women changed.

context_notes.text: Tisiphone is one of the three Furies, avenging spirits who torment wrongdoers; Juno uses her as an agent of madness.
Ino and Melicerta became the sea deities Leucothea and Palaemon; Neptune is god of the sea, Venus is Ino's descendant's patron, as Ino was Venus's kin.
Juno, queen of the gods, hates anyone linked to Jupiter's affairs; Semele's family suffers from her jealousy.
Cerberus is the three-headed dog guarding the underworld's entrance.
The Furies (Eumenides) were goddesses of vengeance who tormented wrongdoers, especially those who shed kindred blood.
Athamas was married to Ino, sister of Semele; Juno hated the family of Cadmus because Jupiter loved Semele.
Tisiphone is one of the three Furies.
Juno sends Tisiphone to punish Ino and Athamas because Ino, sister of Semele, had nursed Bacchus, the child Juno hated.
Athamas is the son of Æolus and king in Thebes' region; Ino is his wife, and Learchus and Melicerta their sons.
Neptune ruled the sea after the gods divided the universe; Jove took heaven and Pluto the underworld.
Juno is the jealous wife of Jove, who pursues Cadmus's family because of Jove's affairs with its women.

literary_notes.text: Juno's long catalogue of Bacchus's triumphs, framed as a question, expresses her wounded pride and builds toward her decision.
The queen of the gods complains of powerlessness, which sets up her ruthless display of power against Ino.
The short proverb-like statement justifies Juno copying her enemy's method, giving her cruelty a veneer of reason.
Juno's proposal that Ino share her sisters' fate anticipates the madness, killing and leap into the sea that follow.
The underworld's capacity is compared to the sea absorbing all rivers, stressing death's endless, unchanging intake.
Juno will stoop to enter the realm of the dead, showing how far her hatred overrides her dignity.
The narrator suddenly addresses Tantalus directly, making the punishments feel immediate; the next sentence repeats this with Sisyphus.
Ixion both follows and flees himself, a neat image of the wheel's endless, futile circling.
Tisiphone's shaking of her snaky hair is a vivid, grotesque gesture that underlines her terrifying readiness.
Mourning, Fright, Terror and Madness are made attendants, as if they were her retinue, signaling what she brings.
The shaking door-posts, pale wood and fleeing Sun show nature reacting to her evil presence.
Contrasting bodily wounds with mental injury stresses that the horror is madness, not physical harm.
Comparing the child's whirling to a sling makes the violence shockingly casual, while his smile deepens the pathos.
Juno's sneering thanks turns Ino's devotion to Bacchus into mockery, since the invocation has brought no protection.
The aside about madness explains her unnatural strength and shows her act is driven by Juno's imposed frenzy, not her own will.
This terse line abruptly marks that Juno's threat is fulfilled at once, creating a swift shift to the transformations.
The woman's outstretched hands become stone in the very gesture of grief, so her mourning is fixed permanently.
Metamorphosis freezes each woman in her last posture, a recurring Ovidian pattern in which punishment preserves the moment of passion.
